definition: Anti-lock braking system. Sensors watch each wheel's speed, and if a wheel starts to lock up under hard braking, ABS rapidly eases and reapplies that brake so you can still steer.
A ribbed rubber belt on the front or side of the engine that drives the alternator and often the air-conditioning compressor, power steering pump or water pump. Not the same as the timing belt.
A bag that inflates in a fraction of a second in a crash to cushion the people inside. SRS (supplemental restraint system) is the name for the whole airbag and seatbelt-tensioner system.
The engine-driven generator that makes electricity while the engine runs and recharges the 12 V battery.
A sturdy, adjustable stand that holds a raised car safely. A jack lifts the car; axle stands hold it up while you work.
A ball-and-socket pivot, like a hip joint, that connects suspension arms to the steering knuckle so the wheel can move up and down and steer.
The liquid that carries pressure from the brake pedal to the calipers. It absorbs water over time, which is why it needs changing every few years. It also damages paint.
The clamp at each wheel that squeezes the brake pads against the disc.
A shaft with egg-shaped lobes that push the engine's valves open at the right moments. It is driven from the crankshaft by the timing belt or chain.
The part of the exhaust that chemically turns the most harmful gases into less harmful ones.
Burning. In an engine, the fuel and air burn quickly inside the cylinder, and the expanding gas pushes the piston down.
The liquid that carries heat from the engine to the radiator. It is a mix of water and antifreeze, which stops freezing in winter, raises the boiling point and prevents corrosion. It is poisonous.
The main rotating shaft in the bottom of the engine. The pistons push on it through connecting rods, turning their up-and-down motion into rotation.
Parts of the body at the front and rear designed to fold up in a controlled way in a crash, absorbing energy so less of it reaches the people inside.
A flexible joint on the end of a drive axle that lets it bend while still turning the wheel at an even speed.
A round chamber in the engine block where a piston moves up and down and the fuel burns.
A gear set that lets the left and right wheels turn at different speeds, which they must do in a corner, while both still receive power.
The engine's computer. It reads sensors and controls fuel injection, ignition timing and more. Cars have many other control units too.
A parking brake applied by small electric motors on the rear calipers instead of a cable. It usually has to be put into a service mode before rear brake work.
A seal squeezed between two metal parts to stop oil, coolant or gas leaking out. Many gaskets are single-use.
The return path for electricity, usually through the car's metal body back to the battery's negative terminal.
The drive battery, motor and cabling of a hybrid or electric car, running at hundreds of volts. Its cables are orange. Only trained people with insulated tools should work on it.
The nuts or bolts that hold the wheel onto the hub. They must be tightened to the correct torque in a star pattern.
A handheld meter that measures voltage, current and resistance. A basic one is enough to check a battery and charging system.
A thin oil that creeps into rusty threads to help free seized bolts. Spray it on and give it time to work.
A metal plug that slides up and down inside a cylinder. In the engine it is pushed by burning fuel; in a brake caliper it is pushed by brake fluid.
The most common steering gear: a small gear (pinion) on the steering column moves a toothed bar (rack) sideways to steer the wheels.
Another name for the brake disc, common in North America.
The sturdy casting at each wheel that holds the hub bearing and connects to the suspension arms, strut and steering. The brake caliper bracket bolts to it.
A suspension unit that combines a spring and a shock absorber and also guides the wheel.
A separate frame bolted under the car that carries the engine mounts, steering rack and suspension arms.
A spring-loaded or adjustable pulley that keeps a belt at the right tightness. Releasing it lets you slip the belt off.
A valve in the cooling system that opens when the engine is warm enough, letting coolant flow to the radiator.
Twisting force. For bolts it is how tight they are, measured in newton-metres (N·m). For engines it is how hard they can turn the wheels.
A wrench that clicks or shows a reading when a bolt reaches a set tightness. Essential for wheels, brakes and engine parts.
A car body where the body shell itself is the main structure, instead of a body sitting on a separate ladder frame. Almost all modern cars are built this way.
